definition: Wily means clever at getting what one wants through trickery.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word wily. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know wily should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The wily quartermaster requisitioned double what he needed, knowing headquarters took pride in cutting every request in half.
Resourceful is milder than wily — the resourceful improvise their way to a goal without fooling anyone.
Underhanded goes further than wily: wily bends the rules with a wink and a trick, while underhanded breaks them outright in the dark.

Tricky is the everyday word for wily, with less admiration in it — a tricky opponent uses deception, and the word is a warning. Wily carries a grin: it praises the skill in the trickery, the fox working the angles, even while it admits the tricks are tricks.

Slippery describes someone hard to pin down or hold to any promise — ask a direct question and the answer squirms away. Wily is more active: the wily work angles and set traps to get what they want, while the slippery mainly escape. A wily fox hunts; a slippery one avoids being caught.

The old peddler had a wile for every market day of the year.
Wily means clever at getting what one wants through trickery.

Grandmother was the wiliest seller at the fair: she entered the pie contest with her second-best recipe, let a neighbor take the ribbon, and sold out her stall by noon while the winner was still giving interviews.
Wily is trickery in the service of getting what you want, and it usually carries a grin.
A resourceful person improvises honestly, and an underhanded one has crossed into plain dishonesty — the wily one works the angles: misdirection, side doors, letting you win the wrong prize.
Wily sits at the likable end of this unit's trickster row: it praises skillful, usually low-stakes trickery — foxes, grandmothers, veterans of long queues.
Cunning is its cooler twin and can turn sinister; guile names the raw talent.
Where no trickery is involved at all, the honest compliment is resourceful.

Regulars at the park tables warn every newcomer about Ruiz, the wily old hustler at the corner board.
Every move he plays is legal, and he will tell you so himself, smiling.
Instead he wins the game before it starts: he sighs over strong positions as if they were lost, coaxing opponents into reckless attacks.
He leaves his queen where it looks free to take, and three moves later the trap closes.
Losers hand over their five dollars grinning.
Being fooled by Ruiz, the regulars say, is the cheapest chess lesson in the city.
